# translation {.divider}

We know how to use truth tables to assess the validity of arguments written in the language of propositional logic.

## but arguments come to us in English

To assess the validity of a *natural language* argument, we first translate its premises and conclusion into the language of propositional logic.

. . .

Only then can we use a truth table on it.

. . . 

Three steps, applied to each sentence in turn:

::: {.incremental}
1. **paraphrase** the sentence to reveal how it is built from simpler sentences by connectives: 'not', 'and', 'or', 'if &hellip; then &hellip;'
2. **replace each connective** with its formal counterpart
3. **replace the simplest sentences** that remain with propositional variables
:::



# example 1: the British are coming {.divider}


## the argument

> The British are coming by sea. For if they are coming by land, then Paul Revere should light two lamps. And if the British are not coming by land, then they are coming by sea. However, Paul Revere did not light two lamps.


## in premise-conclusion form

::: {.argument}
1. If the British are coming by land, Paul Revere should light two lamps.
2. If the British are not coming by land, then they are coming by sea.
3. Paul Revere did not light two lamps.

::: {.conclusion}
4. The British are coming by sea.
:::
:::


## step 1. paraphrase 

We use parentheses to reveal how each sentence is built from simpler ones.

::: {.argument}
1. ([**If**]{.cardinal} the British are coming by land, [**then**]{.cardinal} Paul Revere is supposed to light two lamps).
2. ([**If**]{.cardinal} the British are [**not**]{.cardinal} coming by land, [**then**]{.cardinal} they are coming by sea.)
3. Paul Revere did [**not**]{.cardinal} light two lamps.

::: {.conclusion}
4. The British are coming by sea.
:::
:::



## step 2. propositional connectives

We replace each connective with its formal counterpart:

::: {.argument}
1. (The British are coming by land $\to$ Paul Revere should light two lamps).
2. ($\neg$ The British are coming by land $\to$ they are coming by sea.)
3. $\neg$ Paul Revere did light two lamps.

::: {.conclusion}
4. The British are coming by sea.
:::
:::



## step 3. propositional variables 

We now specify a **translation key**:

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

::: {.argument}
$p$: The British are coming by land.

$q$: Paul Revere should light two lamps.

$r$: The British are coming by sea.
:::

:::

::: {.argument}
1. $(p \to q)$
2. $(\neg p \to r)$
3. $\neg q$

::: {.conclusion}
4. $r$
:::
:::


## the question of validity

We are now in a position to use a truth table to check for validity:

```{.TruthTable mode="validity"}
(p -> q)
(~p -> r)
~q
r
```

The argument is **valid**.

## summary

One last pass over the natural language argument. This time, do all three steps yourself in a single interactive worksheet. Select your own translation key and translate the argument:

[Open the full exercise in the translation app](https://gabriel-uzquiano.github.io/prop-translation/#v1:)



# example 2: interest rates {.divider}


## the argument

> Interest rates will rise or they will stay the same. If interest rates rise, then inflation will not rise. But if they stay the same, then inflation will rise. Inflation will not rise. Therefore, interest rates will rise.

. . . 

**in premise-conclusion form** 

::: {.argument}
1. Interest rates will rise or they will stay the same.
2. If interest rates rise, then inflation will not rise.
3. If they stay the same, then inflation will rise.
4. Inflation will not rise.

::: {.conclusion}
5. Interest rates will rise.
:::
:::



## translation key {.smaller}


We specify a **translation key**:

::: {.argument}
$p$: Interest rates will rise.

$q$: Interest rates will stay the same.

$r$: Inflation will rise.
:::



## premise 1 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Interest rates will rise.

$q$: Interest rates will stay the same.

$r$: Inflation will rise.
:::
:::


```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
1. p \/ q: Interest rates will rise or they will stay the same
```

## premise 2 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Interest rates will rise.

$q$: Interest rates will stay the same.

$r$: Inflation will rise.
:::
:::

```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
2. p > -r: If interest rates rise, then inflation will not rise
```

## premise 3 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Interest rates will rise.

$q$: Interest rates will stay the same.

$r$: Inflation will rise.
:::
:::

```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
3. q > r: If they stay the same, then inflation will rise
```

## premise 4 {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Interest rates will rise.

$q$: Interest rates will stay the same.

$r$: Inflation will rise.
:::
:::

```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
4. -r: Inflation will not rise
```

## conclusion {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Interest rates will rise.

$q$: Interest rates will stay the same.

$r$: Inflation will rise.
:::
:::

```{.Translate .Prop system="gamutPND" submission="none"}
5. p: Interest rates will rise
```

## the argument translated

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: {.argument}
$p$: Interest rates will rise.

$q$: Interest rates will stay the same.

$r$: Inflation will rise.
:::
:::

::: {.argument}
1. $p \vee q$
2. $p \to \neg r$
3. $q \to r$
4. $\neg r$

::: {.conclusion}
5. $p$
:::
:::



## the question of validity

```{.TruthTable mode="validity"}
(p \/ q)
(p -> ~r)
(q -> r)
~r
p
```


# issues with translation {.divider}

Some issues require special discussion.

## structural ambiguity {.smaller}

English is fraught with ambiguity. Sometimes the ambiguity is lexical, e.g., 'I will wait for you near the bank', but sometimes it is a matter of syntactic structure:

> The British are coming and Paul Revere will light one lamp or he will light two lamps.

. . .

There are at least two potential interpretations:

::: {.incremental}
1. ((The British are coming **and** Paul Revere will light one lamp) [**or**]{.cardinal} Paul Revere will light two lamps)


2. (The British are coming [**and**]{.cardinal} (Paul Revere will light one lamp **or** Paul Revere will light two lamps)) 
:::

. . .

Notice that **or** is the main connective of the first interpretation, whereas **and** is the main connective of the second.



## they are not equivalent {.smaller}


::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.argument}
$p$: The British are coming.

$q$: Paul Revere lights one lamp.

$r$: Paul Revere lights two lamps.
:::
:::


```{.TruthTable mode="equivalence"}
((p /\ q) \/ r)
(p /\ (q \/ r))
```



## neither &hellip; nor &hellip; {.smaller}

> Paul Revere will light neither one lamp nor two lamps.

. . .

There are at least two interpretations with identical truth conditions:

::: {.incremental}
1. (Paul Revere will **not** light one lamp [**and**]{.cardinal} Paul Revere will **not** light two lamps)


2. It is [**not**]{.cardinal} the case that (Paul Revere will light one **or** two lamps)
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.argument}
$p$: Paul Revere lights one lamp.

$q$: Paul Revere lights two lamps.
:::
:::

```{.TruthTable mode="equivalence"}
(~p /\ ~q)
~(p \/ q)
```

## &hellip; only if &hellip; versus &hellip; if &hellip; {.smaller}


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
&hellip; **only if** &hellip;

> Paul Revere will light two lamps *only if* the British come by sea.


::: {.argument}
[**If**]{.cardinal} Paul Revere lights two lamps, [**then**]{.cardinal} the British must have come by sea.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.argument}
$p$: The British come by sea.

$q$: Paul Revere lights two lamps.
:::
:::


$$
p \to q
$$
Coming by sea is **necessary** for lighting two lamps. Compare:

>I will win the lottery *only if* I buy a ticket.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
&hellip; **if** &hellip;

> Paul Revere will light two lamps *if* the British come by sea.

::: {.argument}
[**If**]{.cardinal} the British come by sea, [**then**]{.cardinal} Paul Revere lights two lamps.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.argument}
$p$: The British come by sea.

$q$: Paul Revere lights two lamps.
:::
:::


$$
q \to p
$$
Coming by sea is **sufficient** for lighting two lamps. Compare:

>I will win the lottery *if* I buy a ticket.


:::
:::
:::


## &hellip; if, and only if, &hellip; {.smaller}

> Paul Revere will light two lamps if, and only if, the British are coming by sea.

. . .

A conjunction of the two conditionals from the previous slide:

::: {.argument}
(Paul Revere will light two lamps [**if**]{.cardinal} the British are coming by sea) [**and**]{.cardinal} (Paul Revere will light two lamps [**only if**]{.cardinal} the British are coming by sea)
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.argument}
$p$: The British come by sea.

$q$: Paul Revere lights two lamps.
:::
:::

$$
(q \to p) \wedge (p \to q)
$$

. . .

We abbreviate formulas of this form with $\leftrightarrow$:
$$
(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) := (\varphi \to \psi) \wedge (\psi \to \varphi)
$$



## unless {.smaller}

> Paul Revere will light one lamp unless the British are coming by sea.


. . .

Two equivalent paraphrases:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.argument}
[**If**]{.cardinal} the British are **not** coming by sea, [**then**]{.cardinal} Paul Revere lights one lamp.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.argument}
$p$: The British come by sea.

$q$: Paul Revere lights two lamps.
:::
:::


$$
\neg p \to q
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}

::: {.argument}
Paul Revere lights one lamp [**or**]{.cardinal} the British are coming by sea.
::: 

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.argument}
$p$: The British come by sea.

$q$: Paul Revere lights two lamps.
:::
:::

$$
p \vee q
$$
:::
:::
:::
